text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Swedish homeowners celebrating the recent fall in mortgage rates could be in for a nasty hangover unless they have informed tax authorities they are no longer entitled to such heavy tax relief as in the past.

- Sam Nilsson, head of Sweden's two state-owned TV channels, says there is no reason to renew programming policy. The channels will continue to concentrate on news, sport, Swedish drama and children's programmes.

- The Centre Party, the Christian Democrats and the powerful Social Democratic youth movement all rebuffed an offer from the Left Party to create a united front among opponents of nuclear power in the ongoing discussions on the future of the programme.
- MBDB, a new form of party drug Ecstasy, is not yet covered by Swedish narcotics legislation, and the police have been forced to drop charges against several drugs dealers caught selling the drug.

- The Swedish government and commercial TV station TV4 have signed a new five-year deal allowing TV4 to continue broadcasting over the terrestrial network for another five years. One condition is that TV4 continues to make programmes on a regional basis.

- Insurer Trygg-Hansa is to start a new mutual life insurance company with effect from the turn of the year. The new company will be run in parallel with the old Trygg-Hansa Liv in 1997, after which the old life insurance company will be closed to new groups.

- Dutch electronics giant Philips has clashed with Swedish environmental authorities, which has prevented Philips' products from going on sale until environmentally approved. However the Dutch group says Swedish law has been misinterpreted and is demanding three billion crowns damages.
- The Swedish derivates market is suffering from major legal grey areas. One problem is that there is no legal precedent for what happens when a derivates contract is offered as collateral.
